title: Part 1
text: When the big scavengers leave, you might think the story is over. In fact, the strangest chapter has not even started.

title: Part 2
text: But the real prize remains locked inside the skeleton. Whale bones are porous and spongelike, and inside them lies a huge reservoir of fats.
nxt: By some estimates, these lipids can make up as much as about six percent of the whale's original body weight. The fats are sealed inside the bone, out of reach of ordinary scavengers.

title: Part 3
text: This brings us to the third and most chemically miraculous stage, the sulfophilic, or sulfur-loving stage.
nxt: It can last for decades, with estimates reaching eighty years or more for the largest whales, which makes it the longest chapter of a whale fall.

title: Part 4
text: For most animals, hydrogen sulfide is a poison. But on the abyssal plain, it is fuel.
nxt: Chemosynthetic bacteria coat the skeleton in thick, pale mats, using the sulfide to make energy without a single drop of sunlight.

title: Part 5
text: On the surface of our planet, almost all life runs on sunlight. Plants and algae capture it, and animals eat them. Chemosynthesis flips that story.
nxt: Instead of sunlight, these bacteria use the energy stored in chemicals, like hydrogen sulfide.

title: Part 6
text: Some biologists think whale falls play another role: stepping stones.
nxt: Hydrothermal vents can be separated by hundreds or even thousands of kilometers of barren seafloor, and many vent animals struggle to cross such distances as larvae.

prev: Some biologists think whale falls play another role: stepping stones.
nxt: One hypothesis is that whale falls, scattered across the deep sea, offer resting spots along the way, helping vent animals spread across ocean basins over millions of years. The idea is still debated.
